Communion means a deep, intimate sense of sharing and togetherness — a connection so strong that it feels like two or more things (people, a person and God, people and nature) have become one in spirit, feeling, or purpose.

It is never a shallow or casual connection. Communion describes the deepest kind of union possible between beings.
Meaning 1: A profound sense of togetherness (general use)

In everyday language, communion refers to a state of deep mutual understanding or closeness — an experience where you feel truly at one with someone or something, as if the usual distance between two separate beings has dissolved.

This is the kind of feeling that goes beyond words. You can be in communion with another person without saying a single thing, simply because you understand each other so completely.

Examples:

  • "The two old friends sat by the river in silent communion, no words needed."
  • "She found communion with nature during long walks in the mountains."
  • "The grief brought the whole community into communion — they all felt the same loss."

Notice the phrase "in communion with" — this is the most natural way the word is used in this sense. It signals a shared inner state, not just physical closeness.
Meaning 2: Holy Communion — the Christian religious ritual

This is the most widely known use of the word in many parts of the world. Communion (often written with a capital C, or called Holy Communion or the Lord's Supper) refers to a sacred Christian religious ceremony.

Here is what it involves and why it matters:

In the Bible, on the night before Jesus was crucified, he shared a final meal — known as the Last Supper — with his disciples. He took bread, broke it, and said it represented his body. He took wine and said it represented his blood. He told his followers to continue doing this in remembrance of him.

Christians all over the world repeat this act as a religious ceremony. They eat a small piece of bread (or a wafer) and drink wine (or in some churches, grape juice) as a way of:

  • Remembering the death and sacrifice of Jesus
  • Spiritually connecting with Jesus and with God
  • Uniting themselves with all other believers who are doing the same thing

The word "communion" fits perfectly here because the ceremony is all about union — between the believer and God, and between all believers with one another.

What different Christian groups believe about it:

Not all Christians interpret the ceremony the same way, and this is worth knowing:

  • Catholics and some others believe that the bread and wine literally become the body and blood of Jesus during the ceremony — a doctrine called transubstantiation. For them, this is not symbolic; it is a true spiritual and physical transformation.
  • Most Protestants (Baptists, Methodists, Presbyterians, etc.) view it as a symbolic act — a memorial and a way to express faith and remember Jesus, but they do not believe the bread and wine literally transform.
  • Some traditions (like Lutherans) hold a middle ground — they believe Jesus is truly present in the bread and wine, though not through physical transformation in the way Catholics describe.

Despite these differences, all groups call it communion because all of them agree on the core meaning: it is an act of deep spiritual union.

In a sentence:

  • "The church offered Communion every Sunday morning after the sermon."
  • "She received her first Holy Communion at age seven."
Meaning 3: A body of people sharing the same faith

"Communion" can also refer to a group of Christian churches or believers who share the same faith, traditions, and spiritual bond — essentially, a religious community at a large scale.

Examples:

  • "The Anglican Communion" — this refers to all the churches worldwide that follow Anglican (Church of England) traditions. They are spread across dozens of countries but are considered one communion because they share the same roots, beliefs, and practices.
  • "The two churches were in communion with each other" — this means they recognized each other as holding the same faith and were in fellowship, often allowing each other's members to receive their sacraments.

When two churches or groups are said to be "in communion" with each other, it means they have officially recognized each other's beliefs as compatible and have established a bond of mutual acceptance.
How all three meanings are connected

All three uses of "communion" share one underlying idea: a deep, intimate union through sharing.

ContextWhat is being shared

In the general sense, you are sharing feelings, thoughts, or a spiritual state with another person or with nature. In the religious ceremony, you are sharing a sacred act and meal with God and with fellow believers. In the group sense, a communion is a group of people sharing the same faith and spiritual home.

The word always points to wholeness through joining — the idea that two or more things that were separate are now genuinely united.

1. Communion vs. communication
These two words look similar, but they are very different. Communication means the transfer of information — telling someone something. Communion goes much deeper: it means a shared understanding or feeling so complete that you no longer feel separate from the other. You can communicate with a stranger. Communion is reserved for what feels like a true meeting of souls.

2. The word carries weight
You would not use "communion" to describe a casual chat with a friend or a brief pleasant moment. The word carries a sense of depth and significance. When a writer uses it, they are signaling something profound is happening.

3. It can be spiritual without being religious
In the general sense, communion does not require religion. Poets and writers often describe being in communion with nature, with the universe, or with the past — this is a deeply felt sense of oneness, not necessarily tied to any faith.

4. "Out of communion"
If a church or person is said to be out of communion with another, it means the bond has been broken — they no longer recognize each other as sharing the same faith. This is a serious and formal statement in religious contexts.

Communion (noun) means:

  1. A deep, intimate sense of togetherness or union — felt between people, or between a person and nature, God, or the universe. Used in the phrase "in communion with."
  2. Holy Communion — the Christian religious ceremony of eating bread and drinking wine in remembrance of Jesus and as an act of spiritual union with God and fellow believers.
  3. A body of Christian churches or believers who share the same faith and are officially united — as in "the Anglican Communion."

The thread running through all three: union through sharing something deep and meaningful.
